w: Started life in 1750 as a Spanish physician's summer house on the Pasig River, then got drafted into running a country. Malacanang has been stormed by revolution (1986's People Power), buzzed by fighter planes during a coup attempt, and rioted outside more than once -- the palace power keeps choosing.
s: Where a summer house became the seat of a republic.
_facts: Built 1750 as a summer house by Don Luis Jose de la Rocha Camina
seized in the 1986 People Power Revolution, 1989 coup attempt (buzzed by T-28 Trojans), 2001 Manila riots, EDSA III riots
official residence and workplace of the president of the Philippines

w: Finished in 1607 inside the walls of Intramuros, this is the oldest stone church left standing in the country. It survived long enough to be grouped by UNESCO in 1993 with three other Spanish-era churches as a single World Heritage listing, and was named a National Historical Landmark in 1976.
s: The oldest stone church in the Philippines, still standing.
_facts: Completed 1607, oldest stone church in the Philippines
UNESCO World Heritage Site 1993 as part of Baroque Churches of the Philippines
National Historical Landmark 1976

w: Built in 1909 to rival Malacanang itself, and opened, pointedly, on American Independence Day in 1912. General Douglas MacArthur lived in the penthouse for six years; Hemingway, The Beatles and a young Prince Charles all passed through afterward. Manila's grand dame hotel, still holding the bay.
_facts: Built 1909, opened July 4 1912
built to rival Malacanang Palace
MacArthur's penthouse residence 1935-1941
hosted Hemingway, Michener, The Beatles, Michael Jackson, Prince Charles, Bill Clinton

w: This neoclassical pile went up in 1921 as the Old Legislative Building and hosted the Philippine Congress from 1926 to 1972, then the Senate after that. Only in 1998 did it become an art museum, its former debating chambers now hung with Juan Luna and Felix Resurreccion Hidalgo canvases instead of politicians.
s: Where Congress once sat, now hung with Luna and Hidalgo.
_facts: Neoclassical building 1921, Old Legislative Building
housed Congress 1926-1972 and Senate 1987-1997
became art museum 1998, houses Juan Luna and Felix Resurreccion Hidalgo works

w: Founded in 1596 to serve Chinese converts to Christianity, burned by British bombardment in 1762, rebuilt in granite by 1852, then gutted again in WWII -- only the facade and octagonal belfry survived. What's left is a shrine to San Lorenzo Ruiz, the first Filipino saint, raised to Minor Basilica in 1992.
s: Shrine to the first Filipino saint, rebuilt twice over.
_facts: Founded 1596 by the Order of Preachers for Chinese converts
destroyed 1762 by British bombardment, rebuilt in granite by 1852
WWII left only the facade and belfry standing
Minor Basilica 1992, shrine to San Lorenzo Ruiz, first Filipino saint

w: Founded by the Dominicans in Intramuros in 1587, this shrine to Our Lady of the Holy Rosary -- La Naval de Manila -- didn't survive the Liberation of Manila in 1945. It was rebuilt from scratch in Quezon City, and still serves as headquarters for the Dominican Order in the Philippines.
s: The La Naval shrine, rebuilt after Manila's ruin.
_facts: Founded by Dominicans 1587 in Intramuros
National Shrine of Our Lady of the Holy Rosary, La Naval de Manila
transferred to Quezon City after WWII destruction of Manila
motherhouse of the Dominican Order of the Philippines

w: Tahanang Pilipino -- 'Filipino Home' -- is the official name behind the nickname everyone uses: Coconut Palace, a government building in the Cultural Center complex that served as the Vice President's official residence and workplace during Jejomar Binay's term.
s: The building everyone just calls the Coconut Palace.
_facts: Also known as Tahanang Pilipino ('Filipino Home')
government building in the Cultural Center of the Philippines Complex, Pasay
official residence and workplace of the Vice President during Jejomar Binay's term

w: Filipino architect Juan Arellano gave this Pasig crossing four allegorical sculptures and French Neoclassical arches in the 1910s -- then retreating Japanese troops blew it up in WWII. The postwar rebuild kept the arches but dropped the ornament; a 2019 restoration brought back the original grandeur.
s: Blown up in WWII, still finding its way back to grand.
_facts: Designed by Juan M. Arellano, French Neoclassical architecture, four allegorical sculptures
destroyed in WWII by retreating Japanese troops
rebuilt 1946 without ornaments
2019 rehabilitation to restore near-original Beaux-Arts design

w: Running since 1967 under the Ayala Foundation, this private museum stacks archaeology, historic dioramas, numismatics and ecclesiastical art under one Makati roof -- a two-way showcase pitching Filipino art history to the world and vice versa. Reopened in 2021 after a full two-year overhaul.
s: Half a century of Filipino art and history, privately run.
_facts: Established April 1967, run privately by the Ayala Foundation
archaeological, ethnographic, historical, numismatic and ecclesiastical exhibits
reopened December 2021 after two-year renovation

w: Once Plaza del Fortin, renamed in 1963 for revolutionary Andres Bonifacio, this square at the foot of three bridges is one of just four spots in Manila designated a 'freedom park' -- where protest and rally need no government permit. His statue watches over whatever demonstration is running that week.
s: One of Manila's four squares where protest needs no permit.
_facts: Formerly Plaza del Fortin, renamed 1963 after Andres Bonifacio
at the south end of Jones Bridge, MacArthur Bridge and Quezon Bridge
one of four Manila freedom parks where protests need no permit
monument to Bonifacio at its centre

w: Jesuits founded this church in the early 1600s when Santa Cruz was still a suburb outside the walls; it has been rebuilt more than once since, last in the 1950s. As the motherhouse of the Filipino Sacramentinos, it hosts the archdiocese's Corpus Christi mass each year, ending in procession to Manila Cathedral.
s: Motherhouse of the Sacramentinos, rebuilt again and again.
_facts: Founded early 17th century by Jesuits when the Santa Cruz suburb was established
rebuilt several times, last reconstruction in the 1950s
first mission and motherhouse of the Filipino Sacramentinos
hosts annual archdiocesan Corpus Christi celebration with procession to Manila Cathedral

w: A Mexican Baroque church facing Manila Bay, built around a statue of the Virgin Mary shipped from Spain in 1624 and still on the high altar -- she's venerated here as patroness of childbirth. The district's own name, Malate, comes from 'Maalat,' for the salt-tinged waters that used to lap this shore.
s: A 1624 Spanish Madonna, still watching over Manila Bay.
_facts: Mexican Baroque-style church overlooking Plaza Rajah Sulayman and Manila Bay
statue of the Virgin Mary brought from Spain in 1624, enshrined at the high altar
venerated as patroness of childbirth
district name Malate derives from 'Maalat' for the bay's saline waters

w: For nearly three centuries this walled quarter was the entire city of Manila -- everything else was 'extramuros,' outside the walls. It ran the galleon trade to Acapulco and seated the Captaincy General from 1571, and only lost the coastline it was built to guard when land reclamation pushed the bay back.
s: The walled city that used to be all of Manila.
_facts: 0.67 sq km walled historic district, was the entire City of Manila under Spanish rule
seat of the Captaincy General of the Philippines 1571-1865, Real Audiencia until 1898
hub of the Manila galleon trade to Acapulco
American-era land reclamation moved the coastline westward

w: Named for Rajah Sulayman, the Kingdom of Maynila's 16th-century sovereign, this Malate square fronts the district's Baroque church and looks out toward the bay. Sculptor Eduardo Castrillo's 1976 statue of the rajah stands watch at its centre, bounded by Roxas Boulevard on the water side.
s: A square named for a 16th-century Filipino sovereign.
_facts: Named after Rajah Sulayman, 16th-century sovereign of the Kingdom of Maynila
fronts Malate Church, bounded by Roxas Boulevard
statue of Rajah Sulayman sculpted by Eduardo Castrillo, 1976

w: Laid out by Spanish colonial authorities in 1858 as the Jardin Botanico, just beyond Intramuros' walls -- one of the oldest planned green spaces in the city, older than most of what now surrounds it.
s: Manila's 1858 botanical garden, older than the city.
_facts: Established 1858 by Spanish colonial authorities as the Jardin Botanico
open space outside the walled city of Intramuros
